source.title: Out of Distribution, Out of Luck: Process Rewards Misguide Reasoning Models
source.authors: Alexey Dontsov; Anton Korznikov; Andrey V. Galichin; Elena Tutubalina

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and table formatting are flattened, but the relevant feature-analysis results are stated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports SAE-recovered features in a real reward model, bearing indirectly on V4's claim that a dictionary can recover sparse features. It does not test toy-model superposition or the other versions.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports PRM-guided benchmark performance and linear-probe results, but these do not measure any listed version. SAE reconstruction explained-variance values assess reconstruction quality, not whether the listed superposition claims hold, so they are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses BatchTopK SAEs as a tool to diagnose why a process reward model (Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B) misguides reasoning models. Its SAE results classify which features prefer reasoning-model traces (formatting artifacts vs math content). It does not ask whether the model's activations hold sparse superposed features, whether a dictionary recovers them, or whether features are canonical units. Finding some interpretable SAE features is an incidental by-product, not a test of V4. Superposition is cited only as background in Related Work.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Qwen2.5-Math-PRM fails to help, and sometimes degrades, reasoning models. Probes show reward is predictable from early layers on reasoning traces, and 40 of 50 reasoning-preferential SAE features respond to formatting artifacts rather than math content. They read this as the PRM detecting stylistic signatures instead of evaluating mathematical validity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce the original toy-model experiments; it trains BatchTopK SAEs and linear probes to analyze a process reward model.
record.method_sensitivity: The SAE feature interpretation is reported for layer 15; the study does not report comparisons of that interpretation across layers.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs (32,768 latents, TopK=60) trained on all 28 PRM layers reach explained variance 0.70–0.92 (Table 3). The authors report three features with clear math-content activation patterns (Table 1). These are reconstruction-quality and interpretability by-products, not a test of superposition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction quality and feature interpretability in reward models, as tool-validation evidence only.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 19th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 2: Short Papers
record.problems: The feature interpretation is limited to one PRM and one SAE layer for the reported feature analysis. The authors note that manual feature interpretation is subjective and that they lack the full PRM training distribution.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant rows were left out. PRM-guided benchmark performance and linear-probe scores do not measure the listed superposition versions; SAE reconstruction explained-variance values in Table 3 do not measure feature recovery or geometry.

untested.parts: Toy models, sparsity-dependent transition, and geometry are not studied.
The capacity-competition account of polysemanticity is not studied.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure is not studied.
The study does not assess whether features are spread across neurons, or whether SAE features faithfully recover the model's sparse features. SAEs are used only as a diagnostic tool.
Completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features are not studied.
One-dimensional vs multi-dimensional features are not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V4 'supports' label is overturned. The paper applies SAEs as an interpretability instrument and never evaluates the superposition hypothesis or dictionary recovery. Every row describes the study's own selection and classification of features by trace-type preference.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity versus dimensionality, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, and sparsity-dependent geometry.
Whether polysemantic neurons result from capacity competition or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
The study analyzes SAE features in one reward model; it does not measure how features are distributed across neurons or establish that this is general across LLMs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-PRM
rows.operation_detail: Train BatchTopK SAEs and identify reasoning-preferential features at layer 15
rows.measure: Reasoning-preferential SAE features identified and validated
rows.value: 50 features identified; 89% validation success rate; Cohen’s d = 0.62, p < 0.001
rows.uncertainty: Cohen’s d = 0.62; p < 0.001; validation success rate 89%
rows.note: The authors report these as SAE features that preferentially activate on reasoning-model traces; statistical validation used permutation testing with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.
rows.check: This is the output of the study's own feature-selection pipeline (50 reasoning-preferential features, 89% validation success). It measures trace-type preference, not whether sparse features are recovered from superposition.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-PRM
rows.operation_detail: Classify the 50 validated reasoning-preferential SAE features by activation pattern
rows.measure: Features responding to superficial formatting artifacts
rows.note: Reported artifact categories include whitespace patterns, special characters, Unicode tokens, punctuation, and other presentation-level distinctions.
rows.check: This is a content classification of the selected features (80% formatting artifacts). It bears on how the PRM processes inputs, not on superposition or dictionary recovery.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-PRM
rows.operation_detail: Classify the 50 validated reasoning-preferential SAE features by activation pattern
rows.measure: Features responding to mathematical content or mathematical problem-solving discourse
rows.note: The paper describes three features as detecting expressions, terminology, or discourse structure, and seven others as responding to mathematical discourse structure.
rows.check: Same as R2. The 10 math-content features are a category share within the selected set, not evidence on whether a dictionary recovers the model's features.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-PRM
rows.operation_detail: Measure reasoning-versus-non-reasoning discrimination across SAE features

conditions.value: 108 total across 3 reasoning models, 4 non-reasoning models, and 3 datasets

rows.measure: Features with reasoning preference score below 0.1
rows.note: The authors describe these features as having minimal discriminative power for this reasoning-preference analysis.
rows.check: This is a selection statistic: 99% of features have preference score <0.1, which motivates the threshold. 'Partial' has no meaning against any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
